Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the global business landscape, presenting both
unprecedented opportunities and complex challenges for organisations worldwide. For business
leaders in Malaysia, the potential of AI is being recognised as an opportunity to maintain
competitiveness, foster innovation, and ensure sustainable growth. However, effective oversight
of AI is crucial, as unmanaged risks can lead to significant financial, reputational, and operational
consequences.
Board members need not possess deep technical expertise in AI, but they should cultivate a
working grasp of its possibilities, challenges, and the responsibilities it creates. In their capacity as
stewards of the organisation, directors are entrusted with ensuring that AI adoption aligns with the
company’s principles, reflects its strategic direction, and serves its long-term purpose. This
stewardship also requires them to safeguard the organisation by maintaining vigilant oversight of
the risks, ethical dimensions, and potential liabilities that accompany the use of AI.
AI is no longer a peripheral technology. It is a strategic capability that can reshape
competitiveness, risk, and trust. In

AI is no longer a peripheral technology. It is a strategic capability that can reshape
competitiveness, risk, and trust. In practice, becoming “AI-ready” is not about technical mastery
but about setting the tone for responsible adoption through informed challenge and clear
governance expectations.
While providing frameworks and highlighting best practices, this Primer is intended as a voluntary
resource. Its content is adaptable across various sectors and organisations of different sizes.
Ultimately, this resource aims to begin the journey of equipping business leaders with the
confidence, foresight, and ethical stewardship necessary to lead effectively in an AI-driven future.
BOARDROOM PRIMER TO AI ADOPTION & GOVERNANCE
Introduction
01

This Primer is designed to support Malaysian boards, directors and senior management in
exercising informed oversight of AI adoption and governance. It is not intended to turn board
members into technical specialists. Rather, it provides a practical reference to help boards
understand AI-related opportunities and risks, ask the right strategic questions and consider
whether AI use cases are aligned with organisational purpose, risk appetite, ethical considerations
and applicable legal and governance obligations.
The Primer may also be useful for organisations at different stages of AI maturity, from those
beginning to explore AI use cases to those deploying AI systems across business functions. In
applying this Primer, boards should consider whether AI initiatives create measurable value,
whether associated risks are proportionately managed, and whether appropriate governance,
validation, monitoring and accountability arrangements are in place before material deployment
or scaling.

Purpose and Intended Audience
BOARDROOM PRIMER TO AI ADOPTION & GOVERNANCE

It is often presumed that there is a harmonious understanding of what AI is. However, this is often
not the case. Broadly, most definitions of AI centre on technology systems that are able to
perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. It is important to understand that the term
‘AI’ does not refer to a single type of technology but is typically an umbrella term referring to
various types of technologies within this category.
While recent attention has focused on Generative AI (i.e. systems that can create text, images, or
audio), not all AI falls into this category. Many AI systems are predictive or analytical rather than
generative. For example, fraud detection models flag unusual transactions and medical imaging
AI analyses diagnostic images across modalities to flag potential health risks for clinician review.

AI Within Existing Systems

At its core, an AI system is designed to take in information, process it using advanced algorithms,
and generate outputs that support decision-making or perform tasks. While AI may appear as a
“black box,” it is useful to break the system into several key stages:
Understanding how an AI system gains its ‘intelligence’ will assist in identifying potential failure
points within the system’s lifecycle. It will also ensure that the potential and limitations are not
overestimated. This is crucial for organisations to prepare for effective governance, risk oversight,
and strategic decision-making.

How AI Systems Work
BOARDROOM PRIMER TO AI ADOPTION & GOVERNANCE

08
Data is often considered the raw material of AI. Before an AI system can be
trained, data must be collected, cleaned, and structured. This process
involves removing errors, ensuring consistency, and checking for bias or gaps
that could distort results. The quality of the data directly determines the
quality of the AI’s performance.
Once data is prepared, it is fed into algorithms that “learn” from patterns
within the data. Training involves running the model through vast numbers of
examples until it can generate accurate predictions or classifications. In this
stage, the system builds its internal logic, whether for recognising images,
detecting patterns, or translating languages.
AI models require fine-tuning to adjust them for specific contexts, industries,
or organisational needs. For instance, a language model trained broadly on
text might be fine-tuned to understand medical terminology or legal
documents. Optimisation also includes improving efficiency and reducing
error rates.
After training and fine-tuning, the AI system produces outputs, which can
include predictions, recommendations, classifications, or generated content.
Importantly, AI outputs often feed into other

es.
After training and fine-tuning, the AI system produces outputs, which can
include predictions, recommendations, classifications, or generated content.
Importantly, AI outputs often feed into other non-AI systems such as business
dashboards, workflow software, or customer service platforms. This
integration is crucial for translating AI insights into practical, real-world
actions.
AI systems rarely remain static. They often require feedback loops where
outputs are monitored, errors are corrected, and new data is introduced. This
ensures the system stays relevant and accurate over time, especially in
fast-changing environments.

Agentic AI
Agentic AI systems are frameworks of smart software programmes (known as AI agents) that
interact to achieve specific goals. The defining feature of an Agentic AI system is its ability to make
decisions within complex environments and act independently upon those decisions.
Agentic AI systems have existed for some time, but their use has expanded with the development
of Generative AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) and diffusion models. Today, the use
of Agentic AI systems, which are able to execute multi-step tasks with minimal human
intervention, is being explored in various spaces, including human resources, finance and
cybersecurity. As these systems continue to evolve, they could profoundly impact business
operations, workforce dynamics, and strategic planning.
The autonomous nature of Agentic AI systems adds additional layers of risk that should be
considered in their deployment and use. These can include amplification of existing AI system
risks, such as hallucination, memory poisoning and function misuse. As these systems become
more capable of taking multi-step actions with less human intervention, organisations should
ensure that clear oversight,

09
Hallucination (may also be referred to as “Confabulation”) means the generation by an AI
system of erroneous, false, fabricated, or internally inconsistent content, often presented
confidently as though it were correct.
Memory Poisoning means the corruption of an AI system’s persistent memory by
malicious, false, or unauthorised inputs that influence later outputs, decisions, or
behaviour.
Function Misuse means the use of an AI system in a manner that leads to negative
outcomes, including through over-reliance on the system or through use or repurposing
beyond the scope for which it was designed and tested.
Emerging Considerations
BOARDROOM PRIMER TO AI ADOPTION & GOVERNANCE

The implementation of AI systems within businesses should not be approached as a simple plugand-play exercise. Many organisations begin with enthusiasm but quickly discover that success
requires more than acquiring a model or hiring a vendor. It requires a structured process that
strikes a balance between innovation and governance.
AI systems sit at the intersection of technology, people, and purpose. Without clear alignment to
organisational needs, they risk becoming costly experiments with little value. Without strong
governance, they can produce outcomes that are biased, opaque, or even harmful. Without
proper readiness, they may never move past pilot projects into real deployment.
For directors, this structure should be understood as a sequence of oversight gates. The board’s
role is to set direction and boundaries for acceptable risk, approve material AI deployments, and
obtain proportionate assurance that governance, controls, and monitoring arrangements are
effective. Management remains responsible for delivery and day-to-day operation.
To address these challenges, a disciplined framework for implementation is needed. This may
include the following five (5) key stages. Each

Stage 1: Planning & Design
This stage focuses on clearly identifying the organisation’s need, strategic objective or operational
challenge before considering AI solutions. It requires engaging multidisciplinary stakeholders to
gather problem statements, segmenting them into categories (e.g. operational efficiency, customer
experience, compliance), and prioritising based on impact and feasibility. Metrics for success
should be established at inception to ensure evaluation aligns with organisational goals and
prevents 'tech-first' bias.

Special consideration
Data provenance is a fundamental component of trustworthy AI, as it enables
organisations to trace the origin, lineage, and transformation of data used throughout
the AI lifecycle. It involves understanding the complete lineage of data, encompassing
where the data originated, how it was collected, curated, transformed, and moved
throughout an organisation, and how its accuracy has been maintained over time.
Keeping a robust data provenance record allows organisations to ascertain the quality of
the data based on its origin and subsequent transformations, trace potential sources of

n maintained over time.
Keeping a robust data provenance record allows organisations to ascertain the quality of
the data based on its origin and subsequent transformations, trace potential sources of
errors, update data, and accurately attribute it to its sources.
Given that data is a fundamental building block of AI, its quality, quantity, and
representativeness directly affect the performance, trustworthiness, and safety of AI
systems; poor data quality, for example, can lead to biases and errors, undermining trust
and safety. Defining these data governance and quality parameters during the design
stage ensures that any proposed project is built on a viable operational foundation
before significant capital or resources are allocated.
Board considerations:
Does the problem being solved genuinely require an AI solution, or could it be
addressed more reliably and cost-effectively through conventional software,
automation, or process improvement?
Has management defined clear business objectives, success metrics, and value
realisation measures before moving forward?
Does the organisation possess the necessary legal rights, user consent, contractual
permissions, and data governance

13
Stage 2: Solution Pairing
Once the problem is understood, organisations can decide whether to build an AI solution
internally or acquire one from vendors. This requires a structured evaluation of cost, risk, expertise,
long-term support, and data access. A decision framework helps ensure AI solutions are selected
based on clearly defined organisational objectives and evidence of value. This evaluation matrix
should compare candidate solutions against technical performance, explainability, compliance,
and vendor reliability.

Special consideration:
When procuring AI solutions from third parties or adopting external pre-trained models,
organisations should extend data provenance scrutiny to external vendors. As thirdparty systems are often built on external datasets beyond the organisation’s direct
control, the organisation should endeavour to obtain sufficient disclosure regarding the
types, sources, range, and quality of training data used by the vendor. This includes
verifying whether the vendor has secured appropriate legal rights, intellectual property
clearances, and consent for subsequent training.

Proactive scrutiny at this stage ensures that hidden risks, such as inherited algorithmic
biases, data contamination, copyright infringement, or reliance on unrepresentative
data, are identified, assessed, and contractually mitigated before an external AI solution
is fully integrated into the organisation's operations.
Board considerations:
What dependencies must be managed to ensure resilience? For example, does the
approach affect the organisation’s long-term control over its data, intellectual
property, and innovation capacity?
What oversight structures are in place to manage vendors whose AI systems may
directly influence customer outcomes or compliance obligations?
Can the board halt and reverse deployment in the case of unintended outcomes?
Beyond initial performance, how will the AI system evolve with changing business
needs, data quality, or regulatory demands?
Where does accountability lie in the event of a system error, unintended output, or
breach of the system?

Stage 3: Assess Organisational Readiness
Before committing to deployment, organisations should assess whether they have the right data,
infrastructure, skills, and talent. This includes evaluating data quality (i.e., accuracy,
representativeness, and fairness), IT infrastructure for storage and compute, and whether staff
have the skills to maintain and use the system. A readiness assessment also ensures there is a
deployment plan aligned with organisational processes, not just technical capability.
Special consideration:
Proactive change management planning is essential to navigate the significant
impact AI can have on an organisation's culture and people. Assessing
organisational readiness involves anticipating how AI will transform job roles,
potentially leading to redeployment or displacement, and proactively developing
strategies to support these transitions. Boards should prioritise workforce wellbeing
and engage with management to discuss AI’s impact on workforce planning,
including hiring, promotion, and skills development.
Clear communication about AI initiatives, their benefits, risks, and implications for
employees is critical for building trust and engagement. This also

ding hiring, promotion, and skills development.
Clear communication about AI initiatives, their benefits, risks, and implications for
employees is critical for building trust and engagement. This also involves creating
mechanisms for employees to provide feedback and raise concerns, ensuring that
human judgment remains a core part of decision-making and that employees are
clearly informed when interacting with or affected by AI.

Board considerations:
Do the organisation’s culture and internal policies support responsible
innovation, open discussion of ethical concerns, and accountability in AI use?
How mature are the organisation’s governance structures to support AI oversight
across functions (risk, compliance, infrastructure, operations)?
Can the existing infrastructure and governance model sustain AI expansion
across departments or geographies without compromising control, ethics, or
compliance?

Special consideration:
Boards are encouraged to champion the use of a variety of AI assurance tools,
including algorithmic impact assessments, ethical audit frameworks, and
certification mechanisms, alongside ongoing human oversight. These tools are
essential for evaluating the effectiveness, accuracy, and fairness of AI models,
identifying potential biases, and ensuring that systems operate as intended and
remain transparent.
Board considerations:
Is the validation conducted fairly, for example, through third-party assurance?
Does the validation include stress testing for ethical, reputational, and safety
risks, not just technical accuracy?
Are there protocols for recalibration of benchmarks to account for evolving data,
regulation, and stakeholder expectations?
Stage 4: Verify & Validate
This stage ensures that AI systems work as intended before full deployment. It usually involves
pilots, proof-of-concept (POC) testing, or sandbox deployments in a controlled environment.
Testing includes evaluating accuracy, robustness, fairness, explainability, and integration with
existing systems. Vendor solutions should be customised to organisational needs, and

Stage 5: Deploy & Monitor
Deployment is not the end of the AI lifecycle but the beginning of continuous oversight. AI systems
should be monitored for performance drift, bias emergence, and unintended consequences.
Organisations should prepare for lifecycle closure (i.e., decommissioning or retiring a system) as
much as for deployment. This should include proportionate safeguards for the secure handling,
retention or disposal of related data, model assets and system records. This requires logging
mechanisms, escalation pathways for incidents, and procedures for updating or sunsetting AI
systems responsibly.
Board considerations:
As automation scales;
when should human intervention be required?;
when may the AI system operate within approved boundaries?; and
how will accountability be maintained where AI outputs are relied on for
operational or decision-making purposes?
What is the threshold for AI-related incidents, and are there governance
processes for reporting?
What governance mechanisms are in place to ensure that AI systems are
securely decommissioned or retired, with clear accountability over residual data,
model assets, system access and related records?

Board Oversight Lens
At each stage, boards should consider the key decisions being made and the evidence required to
support those decisions. This includes whether the AI use case is strategically relevant, whether its
potential value justifies the associated risks, whether the organisation has the necessary
governance and capability to proceed, and whether appropriate testing, monitoring and escalation
mechanisms are in place before deployment or scaling.
Directors’ governance duties
In approving and overseeing AI systems, directors should provide active governance, including
setting risk appetite, requiring adequate controls, challenging assumptions, and monitoring
outcomes. Directors should support their decisions with appropriate analysis, testing and
reporting, and ensure that accountability for delivery and operation is properly assigned.

The regulatory environment surrounding AI is rapidly evolving on a global scale, shifting from a
purely technical concern to a strategic, operational, ethical, and legal issue. This dynamic
landscape necessitates continuous vigilance and adaptation from organisations, as the pace of
technological change and innovation means that governance systems and processes require
regular review. Additionally, different countries are adopting varied approaches to regulate AI.
By way of regional context, the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics is a useful reference
point for responsible AI adoption across Southeast Asia, particularly where organisations operate
across regional markets or supply chains.
In Malaysia, there is no single overarching AI legislation or regulation yet. However, a key aspect
of this evolving environment is the need to consider how existing regulations and policies are
being updated to accommodate AI, rather than waiting for an entirely new piece of legislation.
Even without specific laws on AI, the board’s accountability under prevailing laws and existing
standards still applies in the context of AI systems. Set out below is a non-exhaustive summary of

If AI touches personal data at any stage (inputs, training, outputs), PDPA obligations
apply: boards should expect governance around notice and consent, vendor
disclosures, and robust security and retention safeguards. Under the Personal Data
Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 [Act A1727], biometric data is expressly treated as
sensitive personal data. Boards should also anticipate increasing regulatory focus on
automated decision-making and profiling through guidance and related instruments.
Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (PDPA) [Act 709]
Boards should manage AI risk through existing cyber governance: secure-by-design
deployment, access control and hardening, monitoring, and incident readiness,
recognising that AI can expand the attack surface and create additional fraud vectors

Establishes the legal framework for preventing, investigating, and prosecuting
cybercrime, replacing the Computer Crimes Act 1997. Organisations should implement
appropriate cybersecurity governance, access controls, and incident response
measures to safeguard digital systems and information assets.

Relevant Malaysian Laws and Guidelines
BOARDROOM PRIMER TO AI ADOPTION & GOVERNANCE

In addition to generally applicable laws, boards should identify and observe the sector-specific
regulatory and administrative instruments relevant to their organisation and its AI use cases. The
application and effect of each instrument will depend on the issuing authority, the organisations
within its scope and the framework under which it is issued. A relevant example is the Guidelines
on Technology Risk Management for capital market entities regulated by the Securities
Commission Malaysia.
AI governance should not be treated as a standalone technology workstream. As AI can affect the
environmental footprint, social outcomes and governance expectations, boards should integrate
AI considerations into existing ESG and sustainability frameworks, including Enterprise Risk
Management (ERM), internal controls and assurance processes, and stakeholder disclosures.
Accordingly, where AI is adopted within the organisation, boards should ensure there is clear
oversight and accountability for its use, and that material technology, data and AI-related risks are
disclosed in a proportionate manner to stakeholders, without prejudicing commercially sensitive
information.

While individual projects carry operational and technical risks tied to specific use cases,
programme-level risks stem from the organisation’s broader capacity to manage AI responsibly
across multiple initiatives.
A project risk alone could indicate a flawed model, unsafe system behaviour, or poor data quality.
However, when similar gaps appear consistently across projects or functions, they may indicate
programme-level weaknesses in governance, oversight and risk management.
Boards should therefore assess not only how individual projects are managed, but whether the
organisation has the capacity, culture and accountability measures to prevent such risks from
scaling across the enterprise. Boards should also consider whether particular sectors, products or
use cases carry additional legal, ethical or domain-specific requirements.
Calibrating the AI Risk Appetite
Unlike traditional IT systems, AI operates on probabilistic logic or learning patterns rather than
following preset rules. Accordingly, AI risk appetites should consider not only security, availability
and operational resilience, but also the organisation’s tolerance for uncertainty, autonomy,
explainability limits,

In overseeing these risks, boards should align AI adoption with the organisation’s established risk

role in approving acceptable risk tolerance and ensuring that risks remain within those parameters.

Not all AI use cases carry the same risk. Some are low-stakes and routine, while others involve
sensitive decisions that can impact people’s rights, safety, or trust. A proportionate approach to
governance, where oversight is calibrated to the risk of each use case, helps organisations remain
both responsible and agile.
This approach may be supported through an internal AI risk assessment and management
framework. The framework should not assess and manage risk based on the type of AI technology
alone, but on the specific use case, including what the AI system does, whose data it uses, the
level of human oversight, and the potential impact of error, misuse or unintended outcomes.
Organisations are encouraged to adopt or adapt a risk assessment approach that is proportionate
to their size, sector, AI maturity, business context and applicable legal or regulatory obligations.
Where appropriate, organisations may refer to recognised standards and guidance, including
ISO/IEC 42001 on AI management systems, ISO/IEC 23894 on AI risk management, and ISO 31000
on general risk management principles.
The objective is to ensure that higher-impact AI use cases receive stronger governance,

The objective is to ensure that higher-impact AI use cases receive stronger governance,
assurance and oversight, while lower-impact use cases remain subject to suitable but
proportionate controls. Boards should therefore ensure that management has a clear process to
identify AI risks, assess their likelihood and impact, determine appropriate controls, document key
decisions, and review the risk profile over time.

Becoming an AI-ready Board
As organisations move toward AI-enabled operations, boards should first ensure that they
themselves are equipped to lead confidently and credibly in this evolving landscape. Board
readiness is not about technical mastery. It is about understanding how AI intersects with strategy,
risk, ethics, and accountability. A board that models good governance, cultivates informed
curiosity, and challenges its own assumptions sets the tone for responsible adoption across the
enterprise.
The AI Readiness Evaluation set out in this Chapter was developed based on the work and inputs
of the NAIO AI Advisory Working Group, whose contributions informed the readiness dimensions,
maturity stages and board-level evaluation approach reflected in this Primer.
To move beyond awareness and support more structured board oversight, the AI Readiness
Evaluation provides a practical starting point for assessing an organisation's readiness to adopt
and govern AI responsibly. It is intended to help boards identify strengths, gaps, and priority areas
for improvement, while supporting informed discussions with management. Organisations are
encouraged to adapt the assessment to reflect

for improvement, while supporting informed discussions with management. Organisations are
encouraged to adapt the assessment to reflect their size, sector, AI maturity, governance
arrangements, and strategic priorities, and to build upon it as their AI governance capabilities
mature.
In practice, boards may structure oversight in different ways. Some boards oversee AI directly as a
matter for the full board. Others assign detailed scrutiny to a board committee (for example, risk,
audit, or technology), while maintaining clear reporting and escalation pathways so that the full
board continues to set direction and make key decisions. A hybrid approach is also common,
where a committee conducts deep dives and monitors readiness, while the full board reviews AI
strategy, risk posture, and the governance of high-impact deployments.
Whatever the model, accountability should be clearly defined and documented. This should
include identifying which individual or body, at board and management levels, is responsible and
ultimately accountable to the board for decisions regarding AI use, and how existing governance

Aware: Limited understanding of AI at board level; no formal AI strategy or oversight.
Exploration: Initial discussions about AI; potential use cases are being explored.
Operational: AI is integrated into some business processes with board oversight.
Optimised: AI is optimised across key processes and boards actively guide a proactive,
sustained AI strategy.

Artificial Intelligence is no longer a peripheral technology. It is a strategic capability that can
reshape competitiveness, risk, and trust. Boards that engage early, ask the right questions, and
insist on proportionate controls will unlock value while protecting the organisation’s licence to
operate.
This Primer has outlined how to adopt AI responsibly across the lifecycle, why oversight should
be calibrated to risk, and how governance should evolve as use cases expand and regulations
mature. Boards should treat AI risk assessment as an ongoing governance exercise, requiring
periodic reassessment as systems change purpose, scale, data, users, context, or legal obligations.
Practical next steps are clear. Embed principles and policies, establish cross-functional oversight,
build assurance into verification and validation, and maintain robust records of design choices,
incidents, and corrective actions. Use the AI Readiness Evaluation to benchmark the board’s
capability across strategy, governance, people, and technology, and to prioritise near-term
improvements.

Malaysia recognizes that while AI principles lay the foundation of an AI governance
framework, there is a critical need to translate these principles into actionable practices for
deployers, and developers across the AI ecosystem.
The AI Code of Ethics (AICE) is a voluntary and non-binding guidance instrument that is
designed to support organisations in applying ethical AI principles in practice. It is intended to
complement existing legal and regulatory frameworks, while encouraging responsible AI
development and use across diverse contexts.

3.Privacy and Security
4.Inclusiveness
5.Transparency
6.Accountability
7.Pursuit of human benefit and happiness
Ultimately, the AICE ensures these principles are embedded throughout the entire lifecycle
of an AI system.

Pillar 1 emphasises the importance of cultivating awareness and understanding of
Seven (7) AI Principles and any other relevant sectoral or emerging principles or

Awareness ensures that decision-makers and practitioners are conscious of the ethical,
legal, and societal implications of AI Systems.
1.1 Collective Awareness
Organisations are encouraged to cultivate an understanding of the ethical foundations
guiding AI by ensuring that awareness of the Seven (7) AI Principles is actively embedded
into leadership priorities, management practices, and day-to-day operations through the
following steps
Recognising that Organisations may differ in their size, structure, sector, governance

and promote responsible AI practices may vary according to their respective contexts
and needs through the following steps:

Leadership should promote continuous learning and dialogue on the Seven (7) AI
Principles to support a shared understanding of responsible AI practices and
encourage their

n Ethically Informed Culture
Leadership should promote continuous learning and dialogue on the Seven (7) AI
Principles to support a shared understanding of responsible AI practices and
encourage their consistent consideration in AI-related activities across the
Organisation.
b. Embed Awareness into Organisational Practice
Management should integrate ethical considerations into project reviews,
onboarding, and team discussions involving AI projects. Awareness initiatives can,
where appropriate, be contextualised to the functions, responsibilities, and roles
performed by individuals and teams throughout the AI lifecycle, so that relevant
ethical considerations are understood and applied in practice.
04

c. Enable Open and Transparent Communication
Leadership and management should facilitate open conversations regarding the
opportunities, implementation challenges, risks, and limitations associated with AI
Systems. Organisations intending to develop or deploy AI Systems can establish and
maintain appropriate internal policies, guidance materials, or communication
mechanisms to promote a common understanding of responsible AI practices.
Such methods may include, where appropriate, communicating organisational
expectations regarding the responsible use of AI, providing opportunities for
employees to raise concerns or seek clarification, sharing teachings from AI initiatives,
and encouraging discussions on emerging AI-related developments.
d. Model Ethical Leadership
Awareness of Seven (7) AI Principles should be exemplified by governance and
resource allocation set out by the leadership, showing that ethical awareness is not
optional but integral to organisational integrity and trust. Organisations should
consider declaring their commitment to the Seven (7) AI Principles by declarations or
statements.

2.1 Risk-Based and Contextual Approach
Organisations are encouraged to adopt a risk-based and context-sensitive approach to
AI governance, whereby risk management measures are proportionate to the
organization’s resources, AI maturity, and the system's potential impact and scale.
AI risk should be recognised as dynamic and context-dependent, and may evolve over
time due to changes in system design, deployment environment, or intended use. Prior
to deployment, Organisations may consider conducting a self-assessment to determine
the level and nature of risk presented by the AI Use Case and implement proportionate
measures to mitigate identified risks
Pillar 2: AI Risk
Management
Pillar 2 establishes a structured and proportionate approach to identifying, assessing,
and managing risks throughout the AI lifecycle. This pillar aims to support organisations
in anticipating and mitigating potential harms and unintended consequences, while
promoting the safe, responsible, and trustworthy use of AI Systems in alignment with
ethical, legal, and societal considerations.

2.2 AI Risk Assessment Guidance
A structured risk assessment process can support organisations in identifying, analysing,
and evaluating risks associated with AI Systems. Risk assessment can be conducted
throughout the AI lifecycle and should consider relevant technical, operational, legal,
ethical, and societal dimensions.
When conducting risk assessments on AI use cases, the following non-exhaustive
guideline can be considered and applied flexibly based on context:
intended purpose, use context, and deployment environment
level of autonomy and appropriate human oversight
potential impacts on individuals, groups, and society
validity, reliability, robustness, and safety of system performance
fairness, bias, and risks of unintended or harmful outcomes
security, resilience, and adversarial risks
data quality, provenance, and governance considerations
transparency, explainability, and accountability considerations
severity, reversibility, and scale of potential harms

2.4 Continuous Monitoring, Testing, and Reassessment
AI Risk Management is a continuous, iterative process that spans the entire system
lifecycle. Organisations can consider establishing ongoing monitoring, testing, and
validation protocols to ensure AI systems consistently align with their intended purpose,
established risk profile, and relevant AIGE principles.
There is a material change in system functionality or deployment context;

System performance or behaviour changes over time;
The intended purpose or use of the system evolves.
Findings from monitoring activities should inform ongoing improvements to risk
assessment and mitigation practices.

Pillar 3:
Accountability
Pillar 3 promotes accountability through clear responsibilities and procedures for
documenting AI-related incidents. Organisations can define and assign specific roles
to ensure effective oversight and timely responses to such incidents.
3.1 General Responsibilities of AI Actors
Responsibility for the trustworthy design, development, and use of AI Systems may
involve multiple parties across the AI lifecycle, including Organisations, vendors, partners,
and service providers.
The responsibilities of these relevant AI Actors may vary depending on their role, level of
involvement, and degree of control over the design, development, deployment, operation,
monitoring, or retirement of an AI System.
Where different functions or activities are performed by different parties, Organisations
are encouraged to appropriately ensure that roles, responsibilities, and relevant oversight
arrangements are coordinated in relation to the functions under their control
3.2 Organisational Governance Structures
Organisations, where appropriate, maintain clear, transparent governance to ensure
accountability throughout the AI lifecycle. This involves aligning responsibilities,

nisational Governance Structures
Organisations, where appropriate, maintain clear, transparent governance to ensure
accountability throughout the AI lifecycle. This involves aligning responsibilities, decisionmaking authority, and oversight functions with the correct individuals, teams, or functions.
Furthermore, robust documentation, review, and record-keeping processes must be used
to ensure the traceability and governance of all development, deployment, and
operational decisions.
Organisations could also extend this oversight to third-party AI systems, service providers,
and externally sourced components. When applicable, recognized international standards
and frameworks should be adopted to reinforce security, reliability, and risk management
practices.

4.1 Define Triggers and Thresholds for Redress
Redress mechanisms can be activated where AI outcomes result in, or are reasonably
likely to result in, significant harm, adverse impacts, or other identified concerns through
the Organisation’s risk assessment processes.
Accordingly, organisations are encouraged to establish clear criteria and escalation
thresholds for when issues should be reviewed, investigated, or subject to remediation.
Pillar 4 focuses on creating clear processes for affected stakeholders to raise concerns
and seek remedies when issues arise from the use of AI Systems.
4.2 Contest and Grievance Procedure
Mechanisms for individuals to raise concerns about AI-driven outcomes should be
straightforward, accessible, and proportionate to the level of risk and potential impact.
These channels should be transparent, published, and easy to use but designed to
prevent misuse or excessive burden on the organisation.
Pillar 4:
Redress Processes
4.3 Assign Responsibility for Handling Redress
Responsibility for managing redress should be assigned to ensure independence,
consistency, and record-keeping. Roles and timelines should be clearly stated, including
procedures for

Handling Redress
Responsibility for managing redress should be assigned to ensure independence,
consistency, and record-keeping. Roles and timelines should be clearly stated, including
procedures for internal escalation or referral to regulators where applicable.
15

4.4 Human Oversight
Maintaining sufficient internal documentation, traceability logs, and oversight checkpoints
can support the investigation of AI Systems. It is recommended that reviewers are
granted the authority to reverse, correct, or clarify outcomes where justified.
The form of human oversight may vary depending on an organisation's size, resources,
and risk profile. For example, larger organisations may establish dedicated review
functions, while smaller enterprises may allocate these responsibilities to existing
personnel.
4.5 Documentation and Analysis
Organisations are encouraged to record redress cases and outcomes to identify risks and
improve model design, oversight, and communication. Periodic analysis of redress trends
should inform broader AI risk management and accountability reviews, ensuring that
lessons inform updates to training data, governance controls, and user communication.
16

Conclusion
The Voluntary AI Code of Ethics focuses on the practical application of AI by providing
organisations with clear guidance to identify, manage, and address ethical considerations
throughout the entire lifecycle of AI systems. Anchored in four key pillars—Awareness,
Risk Management, Accountability, and Redress—the Code supports responsible AI
deployment by taking into account the level of risk, the context of use, and the
organisation’s level of maturity in adopting AI.
Key Takeaways:
Operational Readiness: Organisations are encouraged to translate ethical values into
"Operational Drivers", such as robust data governance, ensuring fairness, and
maintaining meaningful human oversight.
Proactive Risk Mitigation: A risk-based approach allows developers to classify AI use
cases of different risk levels, ensuring that safety measures are proportionate to the
potential impact on society.
Shared Responsibility: Accountability is a collective duty. Organisations must define
clear roles from the design phase to the eventual retirement of a system to maintain
public trust.
Continuous Improvement: Through established redress processes and the analysis of
feedback, the AI ecosystem

public trust.
Continuous Improvement: Through established redress processes and the analysis of
feedback, the AI ecosystem can evolve, correcting biases and improving model
design over time.
The adoption of this voluntary Code of Ethics represents a commitment to fostering a
digital ecosystem where innovation and human values coexist. By using these pillars as
considerations of AI governance in individual organisations, stakeholders can contribute to
a future where AI serves as a transparent, inclusive, and reliable tool for national progress.

AI Lifecycle
An AI system lifecycle typically involves several phases
that include to: plan and design; collect and process data;
build model(s) and/or adapt existing model(s) to specific
tasks; test, evaluate, verify and validate; make available for
use/deploy; operate and monitor; and
retire/decommission.
These phases often take place in an iterative manner and
are not necessarily sequential. The decision to retire an AI
system from operation may occur at any point during the
operation and monitoring phase.
AI Use Case
A defined application or scenario in which an AI system is
used to generate outputs for a specific human-defined
objective within a particular operational context.

Release patterns for notable AI models have continued to shift toward controlled access (Figure 1.1.8). In
2025, API access was the most common release type, with 47 of 102 models made available this way. and
API-only releases have steadily increased since 2020. The second most common release type was “open

remaining models were released in a mix of access types, including “hosted access (no

weights (unrestricted),” meaning the models are fully available for use, modification, and redistribution. The
remaining models were released in a mix of access types, including “hosted access (no API),”5 “open weights
(restricted use),”6 and “open weights (noncommercial).” The “unknown” designation refers to models that
have unclear or undisclosed access types, and “unreleased” models remain proprietary, accessible only to
their developers or select partners.
Training code is becoming even less accessible than model code overall (Figure 1.1.9). In 2025, 81 of 102
notable models were released without their corresponding training code, compared to 4 that made their
code “open source.” In 2020, models with open source and unreleased training code were about the same in
number, but by 2023, the majority were unreleased and the gap has continued to widen. This growing opacity
limits the ability of external researchers to reproduce results, audit development, and validate safety claims.

Will Models Run Out of Data?
1.1 NOTABLE AI MODELS | RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT | AI INDEX REPORT 2026
Last year, the AI Index highlighted concerns around data bottlenecks and the sustainability of the scaling
approach as it relates to training data. Leading AI researchers have publicly claimed that the available pool
of high-quality human text and web data for training large models has been exhausted, a state often referred
to as “peak data.” This has continued to raise industry-wide concerns about the sustainability of scaling laws,
which have historically depended on ever-larger datasets. One set of projections from Epoch AI suggests
that, under certain assumptions, the estimated depletion date could fall between 2026 and 2032.
Synthetic Data in Pre-training
Limits on the availability of real-world data may be less consequential if synthetic data (data generated by AI
systems) can be used to improve the performance of subsequent models. Previous editions of the AI Index
found no definitive evidence that synthetic data improves model performance during the pre-training phase.10
The 2024 report referenced research suggesting that model performance can collapse when

found no definitive evidence that synthetic data improves model performance during the pre-training phase.10
The 2024 report referenced research suggesting that model performance can collapse when real training
data is replaced with synthetic data. The 2025 report noted more recent findings that such collapse can be
avoided if real data remains part of the training set, but that simply adding more data does not necessarily
lead to performance gains.
The consensus remains largely unchanged. There is still no definitive evidence that synthetic data can fully
offset real-data depletion in pre-training contexts. However, recent research suggests that synthetic data
may offer value in more limited settings. Hybrid training approaches, which combine real and synthetic data,
can significantly accelerate training, sometimes by a factor of five to 10 at scale, without surpassing real
data in final model performance. Training on purely synthetic data has shown promise for smaller models or
narrowly defined tasks, such as classification, code generation, or work in low-resource languages, but these
gains have not generalized to large, general-purpose language models. Where synthetic-only

narrowly defined tasks, such as classification, code generation, or work in low-resource languages, but these

achieved performance comparable to real data, it has typically involved substantially smaller models that are
not directly comparable to current state-of-the-art systems. For example, the SYNTHLLM family of models,
trained entirely on synthetic data, achieves strong results yet still lags behind leading models on major
benchmarks (Figure 1.1.15).

Data-centric Methods
Discussions on data availability often overlook an important shift in recent AI research. Performance gains
are increasingly driven by improving the quality of existing datasets, not by acquiring more. Rather than
scaling data indiscriminately, researchers are spending more effort in pruning, curating, and refining training
inputs. Data-centric methods emphasize performance improvements through practices such as cleaning
labels, deduplicating samples, and constructing higher-quality datasets. A growing body of research shows
that training models on low-quality or polluted data can significantly degrade performance. Likewise, recent
evidence illustrates that data pruning, selecting the most informative training inputs, often outperforms
approaches that train on all available data indiscriminately.

FP16 and Tensor-FP16/BF16 now show the highest performance levels and have become standard in many
training and inference settings.

AI Infrastructure: Beyond GPUs
Modern AI data centers depend on a combination of compute, storage, communications, and specialized
hardware that enables AI systems to run at large scale. GPUs and custom accelerators such as Tensor
Processing Units (TPUs) are the most widely discussed, but they are only one layer of a broader infrastructure
stack. All data processed by these chips is held in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which supports moving
large volumes of data in and out efficiently. The leading manufacturers of HBM are SK Hynix (South Korea),
Samsung (South Korea), and Micron (USA). During training, GPUs

large volumes of data in and out efficiently. The leading manufacturers of HBM are SK Hynix (South Korea),
Samsung (South Korea), and Micron (USA). During training, GPUs must continuously share data with one
another, which requires fast, high throughput network connectivity achieved with fiber-optic cables running
high-bandwidth networking architectures such as InfiniBand.
The supply chain behind this hardware adds another dimension. Companies like Nvidia and SK Hynix
design but do not manufacture chips. Instead, they provide designs to specialized semiconductor foundries,
primarily the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and Samsung Foundry, which fabricate
the chips at the nanometer scales modern AI hardware requires. The fabricated chips are then packaged and
tested by assembly companies such as ASE Group (Taiwan) and Amkor Technology (United States). TSMC
is a single point of dependency in the global AI supply chain, as it fabricates virtually every leading AI chip,
including Nvidia’s Blackwell GPUs and AMD’s MI300X. There are high barriers to entry at every layer—

This section examines those costs
across three areas of AI development:

energy usage. The analysis draws from

Training
Leading machine learning hardware has grown more efficient since 2016, as measured in FLOP/s per watt
(Figure 1.4.1). Leading chips deliver about 10 times more computation per watt than those available a decade
ago, with Nvidia B200 and Google TPU v5e among the most efficient. However, models have scaled faster
than efficiency has improved, so total power required to train frontier systems has continued to increase.
Total power draw for training models has grown by several

However, models have scaled faster
than efficiency has improved, so total power required to train frontier systems has continued to increase.
Total power draw for training models has grown by several orders of magnitude since the early 2010s (Figure
1.4.2). The most compute-intensive models in the data set, such as Grok 3 and Llama 4 Behemoth, required
upward of 100 million watts during training. Due to limited disclosure by their developers, power draw
information is not available for many of the newest models that have been released.
Carbon emissions from training have increased even more sharply (Figure 1.4.3). Training AlexNet in 2012
produced an estimated 0.01 tons of CO2 equivalent, while training Grok 4 in 2025 produced about 72,816
tons. To put this into context, that is more than the lifetime carbon emissions of an average car (63 tons).
Larger models generally produce more emissions but not always, as it can also depend on hardware
efficiency, training duration, and the carbon intensity of the energy sources used. DeepSeek v3, for example,
produced approximately 597 tons, which is much less than models of comparable size (Figure 1.4.4).

Inference
Training costs have typically received the most attention, but inference represents a growing share of AI’s
total energy footprint. Once a model is deployed at scale, the cumulative energy required to serve queries
can exceed the one-time cost of training within months.
Recent benchmarking by Jegham et al. (2025) provides per model estimates of inference energy consumption
and carbon emissions for medium-length prompts (defined as approximately 1,000 input tokens and 1,000
output tokens). Among the top 15 models by energy consumption in 2025, DeepSeek V3.2 Exp and DeepSeek
V3.2 consumed the most per query (23 Wh), followed by GPT-5 (high) at 21.9 Wh (Figure 1.4.5). Models
such as Claude 4 Opus and GPT-5 min (medium) sit at the lower end, consuming between 5 and 6 Wh.
When ranked by carbon emissions, the models also follow a similar pattern (Figure 1.4.6). DeepSeek V3.2
Exp and DeepSeek V3.2 produced the highest per medium-length prompt, approximately 14 grams of CO2
equivalent each. For comparison, Claude 4 Opus and Mistral Medium 3 were the lowest at 1.6 and 1.5 grams,

The power demands of models and queries add up to a much larger infrastructure footprint. The estimated
power demand from AI accelerator modules reached approximately 5,200 MW cumulatively through 2024
(Figure 1.4.9). Nvidia accounted for the largest share, which is consistent with the company’s leading position
in global AI chip capacity (as discussed in Section 1.2). When including the full systems supporting those
accelerators (servers, cooling, networking), estimated demand reached approximately 9,400 MW (Figure
1.4.10). However, these figures from de Vries and Gao (2025) carry uncertainty from variation in utilization
rates and facility-level efficiency, as reflected in the error bars on the charts.

national electricity consumption of Switzerland or Austria, and roughly half that of Bitcoin mining (Figure
1.4.11). Excluding crypto, global data centers accounted for the highest estimated power demand at around

maintain them. Open-source platforms like GitHub and Hugging Face offer a different view that captures the

academic publications or frontier model releases. The AI Index analyzes data from both platforms16 to better
understand how open-source AI development is evolving over time.

1 RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT | AI INDEX REPORT 2026
The first half of this chapter tracked the models, infrastructure, and energy behind AI development. This
section shifts to research output, specifically English-language AI publications and citations. Publications
offer a longitudinal signal of AI research activity at scale, and the AI Index has tracked them consistently over
time. While publication volume is not a measure of research quality, and not all research appears in indexed
databases, this approach offers a consistent method for tracking the research frontier year over year. The

Globally, the number of granted AI patents has grown exponentially, from 3,866 in 2010 to 131,121 in 2024

Forward Citations Flow
When newly filed patents reference earlier ones,
those references are called forward citations.
These are often used as a proxy for influence, since
they indicate how often an invention informs later
work. By this measure, the United States accounts
for over half of all AI patent forward citations, a
signal of downstream influence that contrasts with
its 12.1% share of patent volume (Figure 1.7.5). China
ranks second despite producing the largest volume
of patents by a wide margin. The relationship
between forward citations and technological
impact is not straightforward and has been called
into question (Higham et al., 2021). There is also
a strong home bias across all

Speed of Knowledge Diffusion
Patent citation lag—the time between a patent’s publication and its first forward citation—can be used to
measure how quickly knowledge diffuses within a discipline. For AI patents, most receive their first citation
within two to three years, reflecting a relatively fast diffusion. The speed varies by country (Figure 1.7.6). U.S.
patents tend to be cited sooner and more consistently over time, with only 19% remaining uncited compared
to 32% to 44% in other geographic areas. Japan’s patents show early but narrower influence, and those from
China and South Korea experience slower initial citation but, after about six years, citation activity stabilizes
across all regions. The patterns are consistent with the forward citation data above, but

Overview
AI models improved rapidly in 2025, with benchmark scores
rising across language, reasoning, coding, and math. However,
evaluations are being outpaced by the progress they were built
to measure, and benchmarks face growing questions about their
reliability. Even with those limitations, a clear pattern emerges:
the gap between top models is shrinking. This narrowing
extends geographically, as the distance between top U.S. and
Chinese models has closed almost completely. With capability
no longer a clear differentiator, competitive pressure is shifting
toward cost, reliability, and real-world usefulness. In professional
domains, evaluations in tax, legal reasoning, and corporate
finance show stronger performance in some areas than others.
The range of what AI systems can do is also expanding. AI
agents are improving, but still fail roughly one in three attempts.
Video generation models are no longer just producing realisticlooking content; some are beginning to learn how the physical
world actually works, progress that could help bring AI into
physical spaces. That transition is still early, as robots struggle

baselines to how competition among leading models and countries has narrowed. It also assesses where
the tools used to measure this progress are themselves falling short. To enable comparison across diverse
valuation tasks, performance metrics are scaled to a common reference point. The scaling methodology,
developed by the AI Index team, calibrates each benchmark so that the best-performing model in a given
year is measured as a percentage of the established human baseline for that task. For example, using
this approach, a value of 105% indicates that a model performs 5% better than the human baseline. The
benchmarks included in this analysis represent tasks that can be structurally evaluated. It may not fully
capture the breadth of capabilities required for real-world AI deployment. The Benchmarking AI subsection
later in this section explores these limitations in detail.

Third, questions have been raised about the reliability of popular public benchmarking platforms such as the
Arena. A recent analysis (Singh et al., 2025) argues that platform dynamics could affect ranking accuracy.
If providers are able to iterate on or swap model variants outside the public record, it introduces selection
effects that make comparisons less straightforward. The study also points out data-access asymmetries and
shows that additional Arena-style interaction data can improve performance on Arena-derived evaluations,
suggesting that leaderboard standing may partly reflect adaptation to the platform rather than general
capability alone.
Finally, while capability evaluations are widespread, assessments of social impacts remain fragmented
and incomplete. Reul et al., 2025, found that developers’ reporting of bias and environmental impact is
often sparse and declining, while third-party researchers more rigorously assess harms such as harmful
content and performance disparities. Because only developers can disclose key information about data,

The Arena (formerly LMArena) is an interactive platform with a community-driven ranking system that allows
users to directly compare outputs of large language models (LLMs) on identical prompts and then vote on
which they favor. Evaluations are blind to minimize bias toward particular model providers or architectures.
By aggregating thousands of comparisons, the platform generates Elo ratings, a ranking system borrowed
from chess. This approach emphasizes user experience and practical utility, capturing aspects of model
quality that structured benchmarks cannot, including human judgment on real-world tasks.
The user-centered approach does have limitations, as preferences may not align with correctness and may
not be fully representative of model use cases or contexts. Singh et al. (2025) highlight potential sources of
bias, such as order bias, length bias, or style preferences, that are not correlated with output accuracy. As
mentioned earlier, evaluations such as Arena can be a complementary view rather than an absolute score on
model quality.

Specialized Language Tasks
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a way for models to deliver accurate, up-to-date information
beyond the knowledge encoded during training in model parameters. At inference time, RAG systems
augment model responses with information retrieved from external sources.
Standard RAG pipelines retrieve individual text chunks based on query similarity, which can struggle when
answering questions that require synthesizing information across documents. To address the problem, in
2024, Microsoft Research introduced Graph RAG, which enables more effective responses to queries by
structuring source material into a knowledge graph and generating community summaries that

2.2 LANGUAGE | TECHNICAL PERFORMANCE | AI INDEX REPORT 2026
Context windows, the amount of text a model can process in a single input, have grown by almost 30x per
year since mid-2023 (Figure 2.2.5). Models that once accepted a few thousand tokens can now process 1
million or more. At the upper end, this is equivalent to multiple books or an entire codebase in a single pass.
On two long-context benchmarks, Fiction.liveBench, which measures narrative comprehension, and MRCR,
which measures multi-needle retrieval, the input length at which leading models achieve 80% accuracy
has increased even faster, at roughly 250x over a nine month period (Burnham and Adamczewski, 2025).
However, bigger context windows do not translate into deeper understanding, as the gap between accepted
and usable context length is wide.
Recent research points to different reasons for this gap. On one expert-level, long-context benchmark
(LongBench v2), human experts scored just 53.7% accuracy under a 15-minute time limit, and the best model
scored 57.7% (Bai et al., 2025). This is a narrow margin in contrast to the structured benchmarks

the model showed zero-shot abilities in areas traditionally handled by specialized systems. These included
perception tasks such as edge detection and segmentation, physical modeling tasks such as buoyancy and

HIGHLIGHT:
Time Understanding in MLLMs
Many multimodal models still struggle with something most humans find routine, telling the time. Despite
the rapid improvements on expert-level reasoning benchmarks like GPQA and HLE, recent studies show
models have trouble reading analog clocks. The task combines visual perception with simple arithmetic, from
identifying clock hands and their positions and then converting those into a time value. There is the risk that an
error in one step will cascade into the next.
Saxena et al. (2025) tested seven multimodal models on two focused datasets (Figure 2.4.5). ClockQA included
62 analog clock images across six visual styles—including clocks with a black dial or no second hand—and
CalendarQA, which paired yearly calendar images with date-reasoning questions. On clock reading, even the
best performing model, Gemini-2.0, achieved only 22.6% exact match accuracy (Figure 2.4.6). Models fared

In addition to general reasoning, the AI Index tracks planning benchmarks that assess models’ ability to
sequence actions over multiple steps to achieve a goal. Models have to keep track of what has already
happened, avoid invalid actions, and maintain consistency even as problems get longer and more complex.
Unlike single-shot reasoning questions, planning evaluations can expose failures that only emerge over
longer horizons, including compounding errors or forgetting earlier constraints. Which benchmark is used to
measure these capabilities matters, as different tasks surface different types of failures.
Planning
Classical planners like LAMA search systematically through possible states and produce correct plans when
they find a solution. Language models instead generate plans based on learned patterns, which means they
can produce plausible sequences that can have invalid steps or miss constraints.
PlanBench evaluates end-to-end planning by prompting models to generate a full plan from a structured
problem description across several planning domains. A domain is a type of problem with its own rules
and goals, such

end-to-end planning by prompting models to generate a full plan from a structured
problem description across several planning domains. A domain is a type of problem with its own rules
and goals, such as stacking blocks in a specific order, navigating routes, or transporting packages between
locations. The benchmark reports performance as the number of tasks solved in each domain, with up to 45
tasks per domain, compared to LAMA as a classical planning baseline.
No single model leads across every domain (Figure 2.4.9). Under standard planning, LAMA leads in several
domains, including Miconic (45/45), Rovers (34/45), and Transport (33/45). In more structured domains
such as Childsnack and Spanner, frontier models match or exceed LAMA, with GPT-5 reaching 38/45 on
Childsnack and 45/45 on Spanner.
When task descriptions are scrambled to disguise their structure, performance decreases for most models in
several domains, though the effect depends on the domain and model (Figure 2.4.10). For example, DeepSeek
R1 falls to 3/45 on Blocksworld and 0/45 on Floortile and Sokoban. Similarly, GPT-5 declines to 12/45 on
Blocksworld and 7/45 on Sokoban.

Theorem Proving
In mathematics, getting the right answer is only one part of the challenge. A correct result backed by
flawed reasoning would earn little credit at a competition or in a journal. Theorem proving, the process of
constructing a rigorous, step-by-step argument for why a result must be true, remains one of the hardest
tasks for AI systems. Until recently, even frontier models struggled to produce proofs capable of passing
expert review.
As covered in last year’s AI Index, DeepMind’s AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 solved four of six problems
at the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO), winning a silver medal with 28 points. That result
required experts to translate problems into formal languages like Lean and took days of computation. In
2025, Gemini Deep Think solved five of six problems and scored 35 points, winning a gold medal, while
working end to end in natural language within the 4.5-hour competition time limit (Luong and Lockhart,
2025). The jump from silver to gold in a single year, with a far simpler pipeline, marks one of the fastest
capability gains in

language within the 4.5-hour competition time limit (Luong and Lockhart,
2025). The jump from silver to gold in a single year, with a far simpler pipeline, marks one of the fastest
capability gains in competitive mathematics.
IMO-Bench (Luong et al., 2025) is a new benchmark suite designed to measure whether that kind of progress
is genuine reasoning or just better answer guessing. It includes three components. IMO-AnswerBench tests
models on 400 Olympiad-style problems across algebra, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory, with
verifiable short answers. IMO-ProofBench evaluates whether models can produce rigorous step-by-step
proofs for 60 problems ranging from pre-IMO to full IMO difficulty. IMO-GradingBench provides a dataset
with 1,000 examples of solutions and human-graded proofs to support the development of automated proof
grading systems.
Grading mathematical proofs has traditionally required human experts, which limits how many models and
solutions can be evaluated at scale. On IMO-ProofBench, scores assigned by an automated grading system
closely track those given by human experts, with Pearson correlation of 0.96 on basic and 0.93 on advanced

HIGHLIGHT:
Physical AI and Foundation Models for Robotics
Most of what people need help with happens in physical spaces, from assembling products in a factory to
assisting with household tasks. For AI to be useful, it must do more than process text and images on a screen.
It has to perceive its surroundings, reason about how objects behave, and act on those judgments through a
physical body.
Throughout this chapter, the benchmarks that prove hardest for AI are the ones that require acting in the
real world, where environments are unpredictable and mistakes have physical consequences. The robotics
benchmarks earlier in this section reflect that difficulty. Traditional robots sidestep the problem by running
fixed programs for fixed tasks, but that approach breaks down in any setting that changes from one day to
the next.
A growing body of research is trying to close this gap by giving robots the same kind of general-purpose
AI that has driven progress in language and vision. Vision-language-action models, or VLAs, replace the
traditional pipeline of separate modules for seeing, planning, and acting with a single network that goes
directly from camera input and language

n. Vision-language-action models, or VLAs, replace the
traditional pipeline of separate modules for seeing, planning, and acting with a single network that goes
directly from camera input and language instructions to motor control.
Physical Intelligence’s π₀ (2024) and π0.6 (2025) demonstrate this approach, performing tasks like laundry
folding across different robot platforms without task-specific retraining. Nvidia’s GR00T models and Gemini
Robotics take a similar direction, training single models that can control different robots across different
tasks.
The biggest constraint, however, is data. Language models train on billions of pages of text from the internet.
Every piece of robot training data requires either a physical robot performing a task or a high-fidelity
simulation, both of which are slow and expensive. World Foundation Models (WFMs) are one response,
generating synthetic physics data so robots can learn without physical trials. Nvidia’s Cosmos is one example.
But VLA technology remains at the research stage, and the gap between what these models can do in a
controlled setting and what they can handle in the real world is still wide.

The technical landscape for autonomous driving is
shifting in several ways. Benchmarks are consolidating
around leaderboards for end-to-end driving, like
Waymo’s 2025 Open Dataset Challenges, which
emphasized vision-based approaches and are
increasingly targeting generalization on long-tail cases.
Large multisensor datasets are also becoming more
central to research. Nvidia’s PhysicalAI Autonomous
Vehicles dataset includes multicamera, lidar, and radar
data across a diverse range of weather, geography, and
rare events.
At the model level, combined reasoning and action
approaches are gaining traction. Alpamayo 1, a
vision–language–action model (VLA), focuses on both
trajectory quality and interpretable reasoning, while
operating under the safety and latency constraints of
real driving. Multimodal reasoning benchmarks are

Overview
The infrastructure for responsible AI (RAI) is growing, but
progress has been uneven, and it is not keeping pace with
the speed of AI deployment. New safety benchmarks have
expanded, more organizations are adopting responsible AI
policies, and government-backed AI safety and/ or security
institutes have spread to more countries. The responsible use
of AI is intertwined with the responsible use of data, and in
particular with privacy and other legal concerns. There are
also AI governance concerns given the ill-specified ownership
of AI systems, raising questions about whether companies
that develop the systems or consumers that buy them should
be held accountable and what policies each stakeholder
should follow. While documented reports of AI incidents are
increasing, frontier models rarely report results on responsible
AI benchmarks, and foundation model transparency declined
in 2025 after improving the previous year. Recent research
shows that improving one responsible AI dimension can come
at the cost of another, with gains in privacy reducing fairness

Chapter Highlights
Responsible AI benchmarking is increasing, but is not keeping up with AI advances and
deployments. Almost all leading frontier model developers report results on capability
benchmarks like MMLU and SWE-bench, but reporting on responsible AI benchmarks remains
sparse. Documented AI incidents continued to rise, with the AI Incident Database recording 362 in
2025, up from 233 in 2024.
1
AI models struggle to tell the difference between knowledge and belief. In a new accuracy
benchmark, hallucination rates across 26 top models range from 22% to 94%. GPT-4o’s accuracy
dropped from 98.2% to 64.4%, and DeepSeek R1 fell from over 90% to 14.4%. When a false
statement is presented as something another person believes, models handle it well. When the
same false statement is presented as something a user believes, performance collapses.
2
Organizations are formalizing responsible AI work, but knowledge and budget gaps still slow
adoption. AI-specific governance roles grew 17% in 2025, and the share of businesses with no
responsible AI policies in place fell sharply from 24% to 11%. The main obstacles to implementation
remain gaps in knowledge (59%), budget constraints

17% in 2025, and the share of businesses with no
responsible AI policies in place fell sharply from 24% to 11%. The main obstacles to implementation
remain gaps in knowledge (59%), budget constraints (48%), and regulatory uncertainty (41%).
3
The mix of regulations shaping responsible AI practices is shifting toward AI-specific
frameworks and technical standards. GDPR remains the most cited regulatory influence but
slipped from 65% in 2024 to 60% in 2025. New entries in 2025 include ISO/IEC 42001, an AI
management system standard, cited by 36% of respondents, and the NIST AI Risk Management
Framework at 33%. The share of organizations reporting no regulatory influence at all fell from 17%
to 12%.
4
AI works best in English, and the gap is wider than global benchmarks suggest. On HELM
Arabic, a regionally developed model for the Arabic language, outscored GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.5
Flash. The gap widens at the dialect level. On a Slovenian commonsense reasoning test, several
leading models lost close to half their accuracy when tested in a regional dialect rather than the
standard language.
5
AI companies grew less transparent this year. After rising on the Foundation Model

ading models lost close to half their accuracy when tested in a regional dialect rather than the
standard language.
5
AI companies grew less transparent this year. After rising on the Foundation Model Transparency
Index from 37 to 58 between 2023 and 2024, the average score dropped to 40 in 2025. Major gaps
persist in disclosure around training data, compute resources, and post-deployment impact.
6
AI models perform well on safety tests under normal conditions, but their defenses weaken
under deliberate attack. On the AILuminate benchmark, several frontier models received “Very
Good” or “Good” safety ratings under standard use. When tested against jailbreak attempts using
adversarial prompts, safety performance dropped across all models tested.
7
Responsible AI dimensions such as safety, fairness, and privacy are at odds with one another,
and the tradeoffs are not well understood. Recent empirical studies found that training
techniques aimed at improving one responsible AI dimension consistently degraded others.

3.1 Scope and Dimensions of
Responsible AI
Responsible AI refers to the set of practices and governance mechanisms designed to ensure AI systems are
safe, fair, and beneficial and that they perform as intended. RAI spans a range of dimensions, from safety
and fairness to transparency and privacy, and each has its own measurement challenges. This chapter
tracks progress across those dimensions by looking at how AI systems perform on responsibility and safety
evaluations, how organizations and researchers are responding to RAI challenges, and how governments are
establishing policy frameworks to enforce standards.
The analysis draws on a framework of RAI dimensions arranged in three layers (Figure 3.1.1), along with
examples and reference documents. The first layer covers core responsible AI properties—meaning
what AI systems should be able to achieve—including fairness, privacy, transparency, and factuality. The
second layer addresses system integrity and risk controls—or how risks are technically and operationally
managed—including security, safety, and robustness. The third layer covers governance, accountability, and
enforcement. This framework builds on dimensions tracked

enforcement. This framework builds on dimensions tracked in previous AI Index reports while adding new

One way the field tracks the responsible use of AI is by evaluating models against specific benchmarks and
by recording real-world incidents when systems cause harm. This section examines both, drawing on incident
data and benchmark reporting that cut across the three layers of the framework introduced in Section 3.1.
There is not much data available, nor is it detailed about mapping AI systems to the above dimensions. The
analysis presented here draws on two incident tracking databases, the AI Incident Database (AIID) and
the OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM), alongside data on responsible AI benchmark adoption
by frontier model developers as well as third-party evaluations of some of the responsible AI dimensions
outlined above.
In recent years, the number of reported AI incidents has continued to increase significantly (Figure 3.2.1).

Grok referring to genocide and extremist ideology spread across the platform, sparking public outrage and
renewed concern about the risks of deploying lightly moderated conversational AI to large audiences. In

RAI Benchmarks
The 2024 and 2025 AI Index reports both flagged a gap between how consistently frontier models are
evaluated on general capabilities versus how inconsistently they are evaluated on responsible AI. This gap
persists. Almost all frontier model developers report results on capability benchmarks like MMLU, GPQA,
AIME, and SWE-bench Verified (Figure 3.2.3). These have become the shared standard for reporting model
capability. Across the same set of frontier models, results are sparse on RAI benchmarks such as BBQ (2021),
measuring fairness and bias; HarmBench (2024), Cybench (2024), StrongREJECT (2024), and WMDP (2024),
measuring security; SimpleQA (2024), measuring factuality and truthfulness; and MakeMePay (2024),
measuring autonomy and human agency (Figure 3.2.4). In fact, most entries are empty. Only Claude Opus 4.5
reports results on more than two of the RAI benchmarks, and only GPT-5.2 reports StrongREJECT.

Factuality and Truthfulness
While responsible AI benchmarking remains uneven, one area where evaluation is maturing is factuality and
truthfulness. The tendency of models to generate plausible but false information, often called hallucinations,
has drawn increasing attention as demand grows for AI systems in higher-stake settings like

uthfulness. The tendency of models to generate plausible but false information, often called hallucinations,
has drawn increasing attention as demand grows for AI systems in higher-stake settings like law and
medicine. Two benchmarks offer different views on this problem. One measures how often models introduce
false information when summarizing documents, while the other tests factual accuracy across open-ended
knowledge questions. Their scales are not directly comparable. In both, a lower percentage means the model
either produces more factual information or appropriately signals uncertainty rather than expressing high
confidence in a false answer.
